title: Do This If You Want Another Year of Windows 10 Security Updates
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Michal Krakowiak/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft is offering another year of Windows 10 security updates, pushing the Windows 11 upgrade deadline back to Oct. 12, 2027.
                                            If you're already in Microsoft's ESU program, your coverage will automatically continue through Oct. 12, 2027 without any additional action.
                                            Other users can enroll in ESU at any time until the program ends next year.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you are still holding on to Windows 10, there's good news: Microsoft is offering another year of security updates, pushing the Windows 11 upgrade deadline back to Oct. 12, 2027. Microsoft officially ended support for the older OS last year but allowed users to join the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in order to maintain protection against viruses and hackers. ESU coverage was supposed to expire on Oct. 13, 2026, but the company is allowing enrolled Windows 10 users to receive monthly patches for another year—and it's not too late to sign up if you haven't already.  You can stay on Windows 10 through Oct. 2027If you're already in Microsoft's ESU program, your coverage will automatically continue through Oct. 12, 2027 without any additional action on your part. If you haven't, though, you can enroll in ESU at any time until the program ends next year. To be eligible, your device must be running Windows 10 version 22H2 Home, Professional, Pro Education, or Workstations editions and have the latest Windows update installed. You must also be signed into a Microsoft account with administrator status. 
Windows users were originally able to purchase ESU coverage for $30, and Microsoft later added the option to either redeem 1,000 Microsoft Rewards points or opt into Windows Backup to get protection for free. To check your coverage or sign up, go to Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update and look for an ESU enrollment link (visible if your device is eligible). Follow the prompts to sign into your Microsoft account and choose your enrollment option. If you've already purchased an ESU license, you can apply it to up to 10 devices running Windows 10 as long as they are linked to your Microsoft account. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The ESU program does not include any new features or non-security updates, but if you want to stay on Windows 10, it's highly recommended that you enroll in the program. Microsoft has started pushing hundreds of critical security fixes each month—a handful of which have been actively exploited zero-days—so you should ensure your device stays protected for as long as possible.

body:
The following content is brought to you by Lifehacker partners. If you buy a product featured here, we may earn an affiliate commission or other compensation.
    
        
        You’re cruising through a work meeting when your boss asks you to share your screen. Your stomach drops. You have something like 15 tabs open, PDFs scattered from bezel to bezel, and four identically titled Excel spreadsheets to toggle between. Basically, your Mac’s desktop looks like your bedroom did in the eighth grade.While a messy desktop and digital clutter can be a source of anxiety for many people, it’s actually evidence of your deep work. Between an analyst keeping 15 tabs open so a model doesn't break and a strategist searching through 12 near-identical files right before a Zoom call, the clutter comes with the work.Running a standard cleanup app to achieve “desktop zero,” or digital minimalism, isn’t always the right solution. It assumes the mess is the problem, and it asks you to interrupt your workflow to fix something that isn’t broken. The fear of accidentally purging a vital draft or dataset is a pain point for anyone with years of research and work stored on their hardware.
An app like CleanMyMac by MacPaw that respects your working files and clears the system junk works the other way around: it's built to go after what's safe to remove, not the files you're actively using. MacPaw, known for user-friendly Mac software like ClearVPN and Eney, built its flagship CleanMyMac app to be a safe, quick way to tidy up your machine.
Where the slowdown actually comes fromYour open tabs aren’t the only thing slowing down your Mac; often, it’s the invisible stuff under the hood. Preview a dataset and a cache file writes itself somewhere you’ll never look. Open the same Slack PDF twice and you own two copies of it. Trial an app in March, abandon it in April, and its support files stay behind. None of it shows up on your desktop, but it’s all sitting on your drive.CleanMyMac tackles hidden hardware weight, OS health, and security threats while keeping you in control of your user assets. The app identifies potential clutter, such as old versions and duplicate downloads, without forcing you into tedious manual folder searches. It then shows you the results so you can review what it found and choose what to remove. The four spreadsheets stay put, because you’re the only one who knows which version is current.One scan, five kinds of dead weight
    
            
            
                                        Credit: MacPaw
                    
    
When you open CleanMyMac, the main tool you’ll see is called Smart Care. Click on it, and the software will automatically scan your Mac and purge invisible OS debris.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Here’s a rundown of what the app  does:Deep cleans: Utilizing Smart Selection technology, it intelligently targets and removes hidden background junk (outdated caches, temporary system files, and broken downloads) while respecting your personal work files.Scans for threats: Automatically scans for background malware and security threats to keep your online life safe.Boosts performance: Clears system memory (RAM) and tracks CPU loads to keep your Mac peppy during intense workloads.Runs updates: Flags outdated apps so you can update them, and when you want to delete them, it clears out hidden leftover files apps leave behind.Declutters storage: Deletes duplicate files (like those identical PDFs you’ve downloaded multiple times from Slack), similar photos, and forgotten large installer downloads taking up storage space.Plus, CleanMyMac’s Cloud Cleanup tool will reveal large files hogging up your cloud storage. And the app’s real-time monitors help ensure you always have space available for new files, PDFs, and research materials.Your working mess isn't the problem
    
            
            
                                        Credit: MacPaw
                    
    
A cluttered desktop, outdated files, and endless email chains aren’t the sign of a scattered brain. They’re evidence of deep, analytical work. What you don't know, and shouldn't have to, is how many gigabytes of cache files and abandoned app leftovers are sitting on your drive.CleanMyMac by MacPaw clears the background weight, so the only thing competing for your attention is the problem you're actually working on. If you're curious, there's a seven-day free trial to test it out on your own Mac.

title: How to Claim Your Piece of Apple's $250 Million Siri Settlement
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple agreed to settle a lawsuit over delays with Siri AI for $250 million.
                                            If you bought an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 device between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025, you may be eligible for a share.
                                            If you're an eligible claimant, it's now time to submit your claim.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Last week, Apple released Siri AI, the company's biggest overhaul to its smart assistant ever. If you have a compatible device running the latest updates, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, you now have access to Apple's AI-powered Siri, in addition to a number of new Apple Intelligence features. For some of us, this might seem like a welcome upgrade from a company that hasn't done as much with AI as its competitors. For others, it's a long overdue fulfillment of a promise. So overdue, in fact, that Apple may be offering a payout to make up for it.Delays in launching Siri AI triggered a lawsuitThis year's iOS updates aren't the first we've seen of Siri AI. Back in 2024, Apple advertised a new AI-powered Siri that could understand content on your screen and pull data from your various apps to inform its answers. In Apple's pre-recorded demos, for example, Siri could dive through your texts and emails to locate a family member's travel information if you asked the assistant what time that person's flight arrived. Apple said this new Siri would arrive with iOS 18 later that year, launching on compatible iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 devices. But while the company slowly rolled out Apple Intelligence features through the iOS 18 lifecycle, this new Siri was nowhere to be found.For many, this absence ranged from mildly humorous to frustrating. Some, however, found it deceptive. After all, Apple said users who bought a certain iPhone could expect it to run this supercharged Siri. You might have picked up an iPhone 16, or perhaps the previous-generation iPhone 15 Pro, assuming you could take advantage of Apple's AI-powered assistant, but those changes didn't actually arrive until last week, more than two years after Apple first announced them. Depending on your upgrade cycle, you could be on your second or third smartphone since then. 
These grievances weren't confined to grousing on the internet. The Clarkson law firm filed a suit against Apple, alleging the company misled customers with these new Siri features. While the company has not admitted wrongdoing, it did agree to a $250 million settlement to put the case aside. And if you're eligible, it is now time to claim your share of the settlement. Not all iPhone owners are eligible for a slice of this settlement. Per the terms, only customers who bought an iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model (iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 16e) can claim a share. What's more, there's a specific timeline during which purchases are eligible: June 10, 2024, to March 29, 2025. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you bought your iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 between these dates, you can make a claim. To start, head to the settlement's official website, then choose "File A Claim." If you have a Claim ID and PIN, you can share them here. If you don't, you can still choose to file a claim online. You can share your iPhone's serial number, though if you don't have it, you can share your Apple Account email address and the number associated with your iPhone. Claims are open from today, Sept. 21, through Dec. 21. How much will you get in the Siri settlement?While $250 million sounds like a huge payout, the final amount likely won't be: The estimated payout is $25 per claimant, though that may change depending on the number of respondents. If there are fewer claims than expected, you may receive as much as $95. As MacRumors reports, the final approval hearing is on Feb. 24 of next year, so don't expect the money any time soon.

It uses a 10th-generation Intel Core i3 processor with 8GB of RAM and Intel Iris Plus graphics, which is fine for writing in Google Docs, keeping a handful of browser tabs open, joining video calls, or watching Netflix, but it's not something I would buy for video editing, modern games, or heavier creative work.Still, the hardware has the sharp 13.3-inch Retina display, the Magic Keyboard is comfortable to type on, and Touch ID makes logging in and approving purchases easier. You also get two Thunderbolt 3 ports, USB-C charging, and a 720p webcam. Apple originally rated this model for up to 11 hours of wireless web use, although a refurbished battery that is six years old may not come close to that figure. StackSocial lists this particular machine as Grade B, so light to moderate scuffs are possible, and the included warranty lasts 30 days.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The bigger concern is how long it will stay useful. This MacBook Air can run macOS Sequoia, but it doesn't support macOS Tahoe 26, so it's already missing out on Apple’s latest major operating system update. That doesn't make it unusable, but it does limit how much life you should expect from it going forward. At $279.99, I would consider it a short-term option for a student, someone who needs a secondary laptop, or a casual user who mostly browses the web, streams video, and works with documents. It makes much less sense for anyone who wants a MacBook to keep for several more years, especially when newer Apple silicon models offer better performance and longer software support.

title: Apple Is Bringing Back an Apple Watch Feature It Took Away With watchOS 27
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 22, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            With watchOS 27, Apple inexplicably removed the app switcher from Apple Watches.
                                            The feature is back with watchOS 27.2, which is currently in beta testing.
                                            Since this is the beta, there are no guarantees the feature could make it to the official build of watchOS 27.2.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Typically, software updates introduce new features rather than taking them away. So, when you install watchOS 27 on your compatible Apple Watch, you probably aren't surprised to see updates like Siri AI or a step counter on the watch face. But you might be taken aback by what's missing—a multitasking feature that your Apple Watch has had for years. watchOS 27 removed the app switcher on Apple Watch As reported by 9to5Mac, Apple quietly removed the app switcher from Apple Watches with watchOS 27. As a result, users running the beta over the summer, or those who updated in September, were likely confused when double-clicking the Digital Crown: On watchOS 26 and earlier, that gesture pulls up a menu with all open apps, similar to the app switcher on iPhone. This allows you to quickly return to a previously used app without needing to dive into the "honeycomb" main app menu.With watchOS 27, that's no longer the case. Not only is the app switcher gone, but the honeycomb app menu has been sidelined. In their place, Apple is pushing its new "Dynamic app grid." When you press the Digital Crown once, you'll see this new menu, which features the apps Siri thinks you're most likely to use. That might include recently used apps, but also apps you frequently use, even if you haven't used them in a while. 
That might prove to be useful. The honeycomb menu can certainly make apps difficult to find, especially if you have a lot of them on your watch. But replacing the app switcher entirely doesn't make much sense: There's no guarantee Siri is going to list the recently used app you want to use on the new menu, so you might be forced to manually hunt for it anyway, whereas with the app switcher, you could quickly bounce back to any app, provided you had opened it recently. This isn't the only feature Apple removed with watchOS 27—the company also discontinued the Walkie-Talkie feature with the update. But it looks like it won't be gone for long.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The watchOS app switcher is coming backIt seems Apple is changing its mind (or coming to its senses): 9to5Mac recently spotted that the app switcher is back as of the watchOS 27.2 beta. Apple didn't make a note of the addition in any changelogs, so it's unclear why the company undid the change, but it's a welcome recursion—though at this point, there's no guarantee it will make it to the official build of watchOS 27.2. If you're hoping for similar news about Walkie-Talkie, unfortunately that feature has officially been discontinued, so don't expect to see it in a future update.
    
        This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.
    

Speaking of which, the only way to try watchOS 27.2 now is to install the watchOS beta on your Apple Watch. That's a risky venture, since you can't downgrade back to watchOS 27 if something goes wrong. Still, if you're really missing the app switcher, you can get it back by enrolling your watch in Apple's beta.

title: This New iOS 27 Feature May Save You From Getting Scammed
description: Starting with iOS 27, your iPhone now has a built-in scam prevention feature, designed to protect you from social engineering scams.
body:
Starting with iOS 27, your iPhone now has a built-in scam prevention feature, designed to protect you from social engineering scams. These scams rely on pressure tactics to trick you into bypassing security features for your phone, laptop, or online accounts. Here's how iOS 27's "Impersonation Risk Detection" works, what it can do, and its current limitations.How Impersonation Risk Detection works to protect you from scamsIn a social engineering scam, a bad actor impersonates an official rep of a bank, government agency, or a tech company such as Apple, Google, or Microsoft. The scammer may even impersonate your friends, family members, or colleagues you trust. They'll try to force you to disable account security measures such as two-factor authentication, or talk you into sharing your financial information. They'll create a fake problem, establish trust, and then pressure you into making large payments. Apple says Impersonation Risk Detection can analyze information about your iPhone or iPad, your Apple Account, and check for signs of an active scam. Once it completes the analysis, iOS 27 will share a risk level with the app that's being targeted by scammers. Apple emphasizes that the app doesn't receive any data associated with your device or Apple Account that was used to assess the risk level.
From there, it's up to the app to decide how to proceed. If an app supports Impersonation Risk Detection, it may add a delay to each step you're trying to execute, show warnings, or even ask you to verify your identity. Apps can use various factors to decide if they need a risk assessment from iOS 27, which include big changes to your account, resetting its password, disabling two-factor authentication, making large payments, etc.What are the various risk levels in Impersonation Risk Detection?Once an app requests iOS 27 for a risk assessment, the operating system can conduct an analysis and place the action into one of three risk level markers (again, Apple doesn't control what apps do with the risk level information):Unknown: This means that iOS 27 couldn't detect any suspicious activity. Apple says that doesn't mean the action was confirmed as safe.Medium: This risk level is assigned when iOS 27 detects some signs of suspicious activity.High: This risk level is associated with significant signs of suspicious activity.How to enable Impersonation Risk Detection
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
Once you've updated your iPhone to iOS 27 (or your iPad to iPadOS 27), go to Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll to the bottom, and tap Impersonation Risk Detection. Enable the toggle next to "Share with App Developers." Now, tap Share with App Developers in the pop-up. Once Impersonation Risk Detection is enabled, you don't need to take further action. Note that when you try to disable this feature, it may take up to 24 hours to take effect. This is to protect you from scammers, who may pressure you into disabling the feature.In the same settings page, you'll be able to see which app requested access to your risk levels, and why. This will show up under the "Recent Activity" section. You'll also be able to turn off this feature for individual apps that appear in this section, but, again, it may take up to 24 hours to disable the setting.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The limitations of Impersonation Risk DetectionSecurity features are only as strong as their weakest links. In the case of iOS 27's Impersonation Risk Detection, there are two main weak links. First, this feature is disabled by default. Most people aren't going to dig deep enough into settings to discover it accidentally, and the feature isn't going to be used widely unless people know about it. Second, this feature also depends on app developers adding support for it. Big tech companies and indie developers may adopt it reasonably quickly, but other developers may not rush to implement this feature.There's also the fact that plenty of apps have already spent a lot of resources building up their own security infrastructure, and they may not necessarily see value in adding support for this feature. Here in India, all banking and payment apps show multiple full-screen warnings when you try to make a payment while on a phone call. Some apps may even disable payment features if they detect that a screen-sharing app is installed on your device. So, really, it will come down to how app developers respond to this feature.Does Impersonation Risk Detection keep my data private?Apple says that Impersonation Risk Detection performs its analysis on-device, and that the data used to generate the risk level doesn't leave your device. The company also highlights that the contents of your email, photos, or messages are not analyzed for the risk assessment. When an app requests a risk assessment, Apple claims it only receives information about the type of action you performed in that specific app. Once the risk level is generated, apps don't receive any additional data about you.

title: How to Get the Most Cloud Storage Possible for Free
description: Cloud storage is likely an essential part of your data management strategy, whether you're just using Google Drive for documents or
body:
Cloud storage is likely an essential part of your data management strategy, whether you're just using Google Drive for documents or you back up everything to a remote service. You can get a significant amount of space for a reasonable monthly fee, but if you prefer not to pay, it's possible to combine free options and cobble together quite a bit of free storage—around 80GB (or more)—at no cost. A reminder: You shouldn't rely solely on cloud storage for your backups. Follow the 3-2-1 rule, which protects against a single point of failure, such as getting locked out of your account or issues with the service itself. Google: 15GB of free cloud storageThe most obvious option for free storage is Google Drive. Google offers up to 15GB of storage per account, though this is split across all Google apps, including Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos as well as Android backups. You could create multiple Google accounts, which would allow you to stack 15GB allotments. Note that Google recently introduced a 5GB free storage cap on some new accounts, though you can get around this by linking a phone number. 
Apple iCloud: 5GB of free cloud storageiCloud users automatically get 5GB of free storage, split across backups, photos, and files, as well as data from Messages, Mail, Contacts, FaceTime, voice memos, and Apple Invites. You can delete content to reduce the size of your iCloud backup to manage available storage space. The cheapest paid iCloud+ tier comes with 50GB storage for around $1 per month. Microsoft OneDrive: 5GB of free cloud storageSimilar to iCloud, OneDrive comes with 5GB of free cloud storage, and all you need is a Microsoft 365 account. This limit is shared across documents, files, and photos—Outlook gets a separate 15GB allotment. Box: 10GB of free cloud storageBox offers 10GB of secure storage on its free plan. There's a 250GB file upload limit, so this isn't the best option for media or larger files, plus you only get access to one file version. Free users do get 5 e-signature requests per month, so Box is a good choice for documents. Dropbox: 2GB of free cloud storageDropbox's free plan is limited to just 2GB of storage, which can be filled with photos, documents, and files from up to three devices. You can also use Dropbox to share files and collaborate with other users, and the service integrates with many third-party apps. Proton Drive: 5GB of free cloud storageProton is known for its privacy-focused products, so Proton Drive is a good choice for storing sensitive records like tax returns and legal documents. The free plan comes with 5GB of space, and your vault is end-to-end encrypted. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
MEGA: 20GB of free cloud storageMEGA allows a whopping 20GB of storage to free users with automatic backups and 100 file versions, making it a solid option for large archives and media. Other cloud storage services: Free storage amounts varyThere are a handful of other cloud storage providers that offer free plans without aggressive ads, major file size limitations, or serious privacy compromises. Other options include Sync.com (5GB), Icedrive (10GB), and pCloud (up to 10GB), though some users on Reddit have noted reliability and customer support concerns with these services. Password managers often include free storageYour password manager subscription may not technically be free, but if you're already paying for it, you may have some small amount of secure file storage at no additional cost. Bitwarden's Premium plan comes with 5 GB of encrypted storage, while many others (1Password, Proton Pass, and Dashlane, to name a few) include 1 GB. How to organize and maximize your free storage spaceIf you are using multiple cloud storage services, you can distribute different content types across each to maximize features and ease of access. Proton Drive and Sync.com are good choices for sensitive files you want to be sure are secure, though you can use a tool like Cryptomator (which is free and open source) to encrypt your vault before syncing to a service like Google Drive or Box. Google Drive, OneDrive, and iCloud are best for files and documents you need regularly, including items that require collaboration and sharing, as well as device backups. MEGA could be a solid option for cold storage—media that doesn't change or need to be accessed often. And Box is useful for smaller documents, like PDF records and receipts, given its individual file size limit.

title: The iPhone X Literally Changed How We Use Our Devices
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 14, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: AFP contributor / AFP via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET, and Popular Science.By 2017, some of us had been using iPhones for 10 years—a whole decade building muscle memory, all of it based around the Home button. Press once to go home; press twice to open the app switcher; long-press to call up Siri; press in tandem with the power button to take a screenshot: These actions became so innate, you didn't think twice about using them—at least, not until the Home button disappeared. 
That was the year Apple released the iPhone X, introducing the device's most radical change since its first iteration. (Perhaps only to be surpassed this year by the iPhone Duo.) It's funny to think about it today, but back in 2017, the iPhone X's single pane of glass was disruptive, to say the least. Where was the Home button? Without it, how could you do anything? That confusion inspired Lifehacker to publish "The iPhone X Gestures You Should Master," a guide to navigating your newly designed iPhone. 
We had to learn to swipe up from the bottom of the display to go home; to swipe along the bottom to switch from app to app; to swipe down from the top right to access Control Center; to swipe down from the top left to access Notification Center. We even had to relearn reachability: Instead of lightly double-tapping the Home button to bring the screen down, you had to swipe down on the bottom of the display. 
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Reviewing these things now, it all seems so obvious, even second nature. Nearly another decade has passed since we published that story, and by now, most iOS users are accostumed to a Home button-free life. But looking through the comments on this nearly decade-old piece, it's clear the transition was anything but smooth. One user complained about how smartphone gestures were making everything more confusing. Another bemoaned how switching between their iPhone and iPad meant jumping between two different gesture systems. Fast forward to 2026, and it's near impossible to imagine going back. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple didn't immediately stop making iPhones with Home buttons—it also released the iPhone 8 and 8 Plus the same year as the iPhone X—but the writing was on the wall. Soon after, only the SE line shipped with the old design, and even iPads adopted an edge-to-edge display. With the launch of the iPhone 16e in 2025, Apple officially retired the once-essential Home button. Though you can still buy and use second-hand devices that have one (the 2022 iPhone SE can even run iOS 27), it's clear the company has moved on, and the gestures once so foreign they once prompted us to publish a guide to their use are now as innate as doing things the old way. Perhaps in another 10 years, wearables and hand gestures will have changed everything again, and we'll look back with nostalgia on an era when we had to touch our devices at all.
